people.resumen: Noble of the Anjou-Hungary dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.
Noble of the Habsburg dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.
Noble of the Pyrovian dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan.
Noble of the Visconti dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan.
Consort of the Borri dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan.
Captain of the town of Milan, 1287–1301. Lord of the Visconti dynasty.
Consort of the Doria dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan.
Noble of the Visconti dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan.
Pope elected after a very long vacant seat. He promoted at the Council of Lyon in 1274 new rules for the papal election, origin of the conclave system.
Consort of the Savoy dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan.
Lord of Milan, 1354–1378 (corregent), Lord of the Visconti dynasty.
Lord of Milan, 1354–1385 (corregent), Lord of the Visconti dynasty.
Consort of the Della Scala dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan.

people.nombre: Frederick II of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: Emperor Hohenstaufen, king of Sicily and Jerusalem, an exceptional figure of the Mediterranean policy of the thirteenth century. His conflict with the papacy and his Sicilian court marked an entire epoch.
Noble of the Lancia dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Sicily.
Consort of the Anjou dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples, Latin Empire.

The victory over Manfredo gave him the kingdom of Sicily, which included the island and southern Italy. Vespers of 1282 broke that dominion: Charles maintained the continent and fought against the Aragonese monarchy of the island.
Consort of the Barcelona dynasty. His career is linked to Naples, Trinacria.
Consort of the Burgundy dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples, Trinacria.
The son of Frederick II and king of Sicily, he defended the power of Hohenstaufen in Italy against the papacy. He died in Benevento fighting Charles of Anjou.

Daughter of Amadeus IV, she married Manfredo III of Saluzzo first and was the mother of Thomas I. After widowing she took part in the guardianship of her son and contracted a second marriage with Manfredo, future king of Sicily.

Daughter of Manfredo and wife of Peter III, he preserved the dynastic connection between the Hohenstaufen and the new island monarchy. Vespers made this inheritance politically decisive. His sons Jaime and Federico show that Aragon and Sicily could share family without maintaining the same sovereign.
King of Aragon whose intervention in Sicily after the Sicilian Vespers extended Aragonese influence through the Mediterranean. His reign opened a long conflict with the Anjou and the papacy.

King of Aragon who consolidated the Mediterranean projection of the Crown after the Sicilian crisis. His diplomacy and alliances placed the house of Aragon at the heart of Western Mediterranean politics.
He made the court of Naples an important political and cultural center of the Mediterranean. His succession in favor of Joan I opened a stage of conflicts between Angevin branches.
Noble of the Barcelona dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.
Consort of the Barcelona dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.

Heir to Roberto of Naples, he died before his father. That death caused the succession to fall on his daughters Juana and Maria; his descendants later led the struggles between the branches of the house of Anjou.
Consort of the Visconti dynasty. His career is linked to Austria, Milan.
Consort of the Sforza dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Holy Roman Empire, Milan.
First Duke of Milan of the Visconti house. Through war, diplomacy and territorial purchases he built a domain that aspired to become the great power of northern Italy.
Consort of the Valois dynasty. His career is linked to Milan, France.
Consort of the Visconti dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan.
Consort of the Visconti dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan, France.
He was the last Duke of Milan of the Visconti male line. His death opened up a crisis that passed through the Ambrosian Republic before the rise of Francesco Sforza.
Noble of the Maino dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan.
The only daughter of Filippo Maria Visconti, Duke of Milan. Her marriage to Condottiere Francesco Sforza (1441) allowed him to take the duchy in 1450.
Count of the Sforza dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan, Naples.
Noble, his trajectory is linked to Milan.
Consort, your trajectory is linked to Milan.
Count of the Sforza dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan, Tuscany.
Condottiere became Duke of Milan after marrying Bianca Maria Visconti. He founded the Sforza dynasty and stabilized the duchy in the Italian balance of the mid-15th century.
Consort of the Sforza dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan, Naples.
His Milanese court stood out for musical patronage and the ceremonial princely. He was murdered in a church in Milan, leaving a minor heir.
Noble, his trajectory is linked to Milan.
Noble Italiana, Madame de Imola y Forlì and one of the most famous figures of Romagna politics. He defended his dominions vigorously until he was defeated by Cesare Borgia.
Consort of the Sforza dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan, Ferrara.

He inherited the Duchy of Milan as a child, but the power remained in the hands of his uncle Ludovico. The distance between his title and his effective authority is essential to understand the succession of the Sforza.
Consort of the Trastámara dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan, Naples.
He ruled Milan first as tutor to his nephew and then as Duke. His policy of alliances favored French intervention in Italy, which ended up causing his fall.
Consort of the East Dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan, Ferrara.
Noble of the Gallerani dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan.
Noble, his trajectory is linked to Milan.
Noble of the Sforza dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan.
Count of the Sanseverino dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan, France.
The Commitment of Caspe chose him to succeed Martin I, inaugurating the Trastámara branch of Aragon. Previously he had exercised the regency of Castile during the minority of John II.
King of Aragon and conqueror of Naples, where he established a court that became one of the great humanist foci of the 15th century.

King of Aragon and Navarre, central figure of the dynastic conflicts of the Iberian peninsula of the 15th century. He was the father of Fernando the Catholic and key piece in the expansion of the Trastámara.

King of Aragon and, together with Isabel I, protagonist of the dynastic union of Hispanic crowns. His politics combined peninsular consolidation, Mediterranean expansion and intense marriage diplomacy.
Queen of Castile and Aragon, daughter of the Catholic Monarchs and mother of Charles V. He retained his crowns while Philip, Ferdinand and Charles successively exercised the government.

Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire and sovereign of a composite monarchy that reached the Iberian peninsula, Italy, the Netherlands and America. Philip I inherited the Franche-Comté, Artois, Namur and Luxembourg, as well as other Dutch territories. He later incorporated Frisia, Utrecht, Overijssel, Drente, Groningen and Guelders in a staggered form, between 1524 and 1543. He preserved the ducal dignity of Burgundy, but did not rule the Duchy incorporated into France. From 1535 he kept Milan under imperial control; the investiture and subsequent possession of Philip II must be distinguished from that government.
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. His career is linked to Ferrara, Austria.

King of the Hispanic Monarchy at the time of its highest European and Atlantic projection. During his reign there were Lepanto, the dynastic union with Portugal and the great rebellion of the Netherlands.
Princess of Tarento, 1463–1465. Princess of the Clermont dynasty.

Alexander Farnesius was Governor General of the Netherlands of Philip II between 1578 and 1592, and Duke of Parma since 1586. The reconciliation of Artois and Henao and the recovery of southern cities consolidated the royal authority.
He secured the continuity of the Duchy of Parma for the Farnese amid pressure from the papacy, France and the Habsburgs. His marriage to Margaret of Austria reinforced those dynastic connections.
Governor of the Netherlands, 1559–1567 (Regency), Governor of the Habsburg dynasty.
He consolidated the ducal authority of the Farnesians in Parma. His government was marked by the control of the nobility and by a severe repression of an alleged aristocratic conspiracy.

Pope Alexander VI, a member of the Borja family and one of the most controversial figures of the Renaissance papacy. His pontificate was deeply intertwined with Italian politics and the promotion of his children.
His election as Callixtus III led the Borja to the pontificate for the first time. He pushed resistance against the Ottoman advance after the fall of Constantinople.
Noble of the Cattanei dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Pontifical States.
He returned Mallorca to his domains and fought against Pedro I of Castile. His reign reinforced the royal ceremonial and left an important autobiographical chronicle.
He transformed Ferrara with a large urban expansion associated with Biagio Rossetti. His court was an important focus of music, theater and humanist culture.
Consort of the Trastámara dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Ferrara.
Consort of the Trastámara dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.
His brief reign coincided with the invasion of Italy by Charles VIII of France. He abdicated in favor of his son Ferdinand II when the position of the dynasty collapsed.
His death without a legitimate surviving heir opened the Aragonese interregno. The crisis was resolved with the Caspe Commitment and the election of Fernando de Antequera.
Consort of the Paleolog-Monferrato dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Monferrato, Urgel.
Son of Theodore I, continued in Monferrato the branch of the Paleologists arrived from Byzantium. His marriage to Isabella of Majorca added a connection to the Majorcan royal house.
Prince of Tarento, 1294–1332. Prince of the Anjou-Tarento dynasty.
Daughter of Alexander VI and central figure of the Borja dynastic alliances. After several political marriages she became Duchess of Ferrara and developed an important cultural court.
Consort of the Savoy dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan.
Princess Medici became queen and regent of France. She tried to maintain the balance of the monarchy during the wars of religion and the confrontation between Catholic and Protestant factions.

people.nombre: Eleanor of Austria, Duchess of Mantua
people.resumen: Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. His career is linked to Mantua.
Consort of the Gonzaga dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Ferrara.
He consolidated the power of the Gonzaga and obtained the ducal dignity for Monferrato. His musical sponsorship reinforced the cultural importance of the court of Mantua.
He was the last Duke of Ferrara of the legitimate line of the East. The lack of recognized heirs allowed the papacy to incorporate Ferrara, while another branch retained Modena.
His court gathered artists and musicians such as Claudio Monteverdi. Cultural splendour lived with high expenses that affected the ducal finances.
Consort of the Medici dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Mantua.

people.nombre: Joanna of Austria, Grand Duchess of Tuscany
people.resumen: Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Tuscany.
His Tuscan government combined the interest in experimentation and the arts with a very personal court policy. The absence of a surviving male heir led the great duchy to his brother Fernando.
Consort of the Anjou-Hungary dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.
Noble of the Gazela dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.
Noble of the Trastámara dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples, Papal States.
Noble of the Falangola dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.
Theologian of the Aquinas dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Papal States.
Prince of Tarento, 1332–1364. Prince of the Anjou-Tarento dynasty.
Consort of the Bourbon dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.
Noble of the Anjou dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.
Prince of Tarento, 1364–1374. Prince of the Anjou-Tarento dynasty.
Consort of the Baux dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Sicily.
Prince of the Baux Dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.
Duke of the Baux dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.
The adoption by Juana I gave him a pretense about Naples which contested Charles of Durazzo. His Angevin rights should not be confused with a continued dominion of the Neapolitan kingdom.
Consort of the Châtillon dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Anjou, Naples.
He managed to occupy Naples during a part of his dispute with Ladislao. The struggle for the Italian kingdom absorbed much of the resources and politics of his home.
Prince Angevin with rights and titles distributed throughout France and Italy. His career reflects the complexity of Anjou's dynastic claims to Naples, Lorraine and Provence.
Duchess of the Lorraine dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Lorraine, Naples.
Consort of the Savoy dynasty. His trajectory is linked to France, Savoy.
His expedition to conquer Naples opened the wars of Italy. The campaign showed French military capability, but also provoked a coalition against its expansion.
King of France who intervened decisively in the wars of Italy. His reign combined dynastic ambition in Milan and Naples with reforms that consolidated his popularity in the kingdom.
Consort of the Valois-Orleans dynasty. His career is linked to France, Ferrara.
He defended Ferrara against the pontifical pressures during the Italian wars. His artillery experience and alliances were essential for the survival of the duchy.
His marriage to Renata de France connected Ferrara to the French monarchy. The reformed sympathies of the Duchess made the court a space of religious tension.
Noble of the Savoy dynasty. His trajectory is linked to France, Savoy.
King of France, rival of Charles V and great Renaissance patrons. The Italian wars and competition with the Habsburgs dominated much of his reign.
Consort of the Lorraine Dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Lorraine, Tuscany.
He consolidated the power of the Medici and conquered Siena, expanding its territorial domain. The acquisition of the title of Grand Duke of Tuscany culminated this political transformation.
Consort of the Álvarez dynasty of Toledo. His trajectory is linked to Tuscany, Florence.
He abandoned the cardinal race to succeed his brother in Tuscany. He pushed the port of Livorno and sought to widen the diplomatic margins of the Medici.

Daughter of the Grand Duke Francis I of Tuscany and second wife of Henry IV of France. Regent for his son Louis XIII after the assassination of the king in 1610, she was banished after facing Richelieu.

Daughter of Henry IV of France and Mary of Medici, he married Victor Amadeus I of Savoy. After widowing he defended the government of his sons against the princes of the ducal family, including Thomas Francis of Carignano.
Duke of Savoy between 1630 and 1637 and husband of Christine of France, daughter of Henry IV. By the treatise of Cherasco (1631) Pinerolo ceded to France.
King of Spain whose government was dominated by the Duke of Lerma and by a initially more peaceful foreign policy. His reign saw the expulsion of the Moors and the beginning of the Thirty Years' War.

King of Spain during a period of great cultural brilliance and strong political crises. His reign, associated with the Count-Duke of Olivares, was marked by European wars and rebellions of Catalonia and Portugal.

Daughter of Henry II and Leonor of Aquitaine, he married William II of Sicily in 1177. Widow, accompanied his brother Richard in the third crusade and in 1196 married Raimundo VI of Tolosa. He died in 1199 and was buried in Fontevraud.
He inherited the rights of the Hohenstaufen in Germany and Sicily in full struggle with the papacy. His death left Conrado, known as Conradino, as heir to a threatened cause.

The Sicilians chose him in the face of the resignation of his brother James II. The peace of Caltabellatta recognized his lifelong government as king of Trinacria, but did not definitively resolve the succession: the permanence of his lineage reopened the conflict with the Anjou.

Her marriage to Frederick of Sicily sealed the rapprochement between the houses of Anjou and Barcelona after Caltabellotta. She was the mother of Peter II and the next generation of the island monarchy. The family bond did not prevent the two crowns from continuing to dispute rights and territories.

Associated to the throne by Frederick, he inherited a monarchy that the Anjou continued to claim. His brief independent government left the crown to a boy, Louis, and opened a period of regency and competition among Sicilian barons.
Consort of the Gorizia dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Trinacria, Carinthia.
Consort of the Barcelona-Sicily dynasty. His career is linked to Palatinate, Trinacria.
Prince of Achaia, 1318–1332. Duke of the Anjou-Durazzo dynasty.
Consort of the Talleyrand-Périgord dynasty. His career is linked to Naples, Durazzo.
Count of Gravina, 1336–1362. Count of the Anjou-Durazzo dynasty.
Consort of the Sanseverino dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.

Charles of Durazzo ruled Croatia and Dalmatia by delegation of Louis I before conquering Naples in 1381. His domains included Corfu and Butrinto; his authority over Achaia was nominal, in front of the local power of the Navarra Company. Coronado king of Hungary and Croatia on 31 December 1385, suffered an attack on Buddha in February 1386 and died shortly after. His title of Jerusalem did not imply control of the Holy Land.

He inherited the continental crown while he was captive to the Aragonese. His liberation, marriage diplomacy and agreements with James II and Frederick articulated the Angioinian attempts to recover Sicily. His sons extended the family to Hungary, Tarento and Durazzo.

people.nombre: Mary of Hungary, Queen of Naples
people.resumen: Consort of the Árpád dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples, Hungary.
Ferrante, natural son of Alfonso V of Aragon, king of Naples since 1458. He overcame the revolt of the Barons of 1485 with harshness and was a central actor of Italian equilibrium.

Last Trastámara king of Naples (1496–1501). Louis XII of France and Ferdinand the Catholic divided their kingdom by the treaty of Granada (1500); Frederick surrendered to the French and died in Tours in 1504.

Ferrandino, king of Naples between 1495 and 1496. He fled before the invasion of Charles VIII of France and recovered the kingdom with Spanish and Venetian help, but died the following year without children.
Consort of the Trastámara dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.
Princess of the Anjou-Tarento dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Naples, Tarento.

He ruled a Sicily weakened by noble conflicts and Neapolitan pressure. Avignon’s agreement of 1372 gave a new framework to the recognition of the island crown. His daughter Mary inherited the kingdom and remained at the center of the struggles to control the succession.

A widow of Charles III, he exercised the regency of Naples by his son Ladislao. The dispute with the branch of Anjou forced to sustain power from reduced bases and to negotiate supports; his intervention preserved the rights of the house of Durazzo.
The titular Consort of the Anjou-Durazzo dynasty. His career is linked to Naples, Latin Empire, Tarento.
Consort of the Visconti dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Bavaria, Milan.
Consort of the Visconti dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Bavaria, Milan.
Consort of the Savoy dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Bavaria, Savoy.
Condottiere of the Hawkwood Dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence, Milan, Pontifical States.
Condottiere of the Barbian dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Pontifical States, Naples.
Condottiere of the Fortebraccio dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Pontifical States, Naples.
Condottiere of the Piccinino dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan, Florence.
Condottiere of the Piccinino dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan, Naples.
Condottiere of the Piccinino dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan, Naples.
Condottiere of the Bussone dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan.
Condottiere of the Tolentino dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Condottiere of the Narni dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Pontifical States.

Condottiere of the nobility of Bergamo, Bartolomeo Colleoni fought for various Italian powers before consolidating himself as captain general of Venice in 1454. His fortune sustained possessions, foundations and artistic commissions in the territory of Bergamasco. He died in 1475.
Lord of Fano, 1385–1427. Lord of the Malatesta dynasty.
Consort of the Atti dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Pontifical States.
Lord of Rimini, 1432–1468. Lord of the Malatesta dynasty.
Earl of Urbino, 1404–1443. Count of the Montefeltro dynasty.
Condottiere, Duke of Urbino and one of the great humanist princes of the Italian Renaissance. He combined a successful military career with a court famous for his culture and patronage.
Condottiere of the Colonna dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples, Pontifical States.
Condottiere of the Colonna dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples, Pontifical States.
Noble of the Colonna dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples, Pontifical States.
Marquis of the Ávalos dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples, Milan.
Noble of the Medici dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Condottiere of the Medici dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence, Papal States.
Marquesa of the East Dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Mantua, Ferrara.
Marquis of Mantua, 1484–1519. Marquis of the Gonzaga dynasty.

Daughter of William IX and Anne of Alençon, her marriage to Frederick II Gonzaga was decisive for the transmission of Monferrato to that house. The inheritance required an imperial resolution and was not an automatic effect of weddings.

Marquess de Mantua since 1519 and first Duke since 1530 by concession of Charles V. He commissioned Giulio Romano the Palace of Te; his marriage to Margarita Paleologian brought Monferrato to the Gonzaga in 1536.
Condottiere of the Gonzaga dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Mantua, Milan.
Condottiere of the Trivulzio dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan, France.
Condottiere of the Vitelli dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence, Pontifical States.
Condottiere of the Alvian dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Papal States.
Duke of Savoy who took advantage of the Spanish War of Succession to raise the rank of his house. He first became king of Sicily and then king of Sardinia.
Consort of the Bourbon-Orleans dynasty. His trajectory is linked to France, Savoy.
Consort of the Savoy dynasty. His trajectory is linked to France, Savoy.
Last Habsburg king of Spain. His lack of descent turned his succession into a European question and, after his death, triggered the Spanish War of Succession.
Consort of the Savoy dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Spain, Savoy.
Consort of the Farnesian dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Spain, Parma.

First Bourbon king of Spain. The War of Succession made him lose Milan, Naples and Sardinia; he recovered the latter briefly between 1717 and 1720. His peninsular and Italian domains followed different paths.

He ruled Naples and Sicily from 1734 before inheriting the Spanish monarchy in 1759. He then gave both Italian kingdoms to his son Fernando. His Spanish reign prompted urban and administrative reforms.
Son of Charles III, he received in 1759 the separate crowns of Naples and Sicily as a child. Revolutionary crises interrupted his control of the continent; both kingdoms formally joined in 1816.
Consort of the Bourbon-Parma dynasty. His career is linked to Spain, Parma.
One of the most powerful popes of the Middle Ages. He actively intervened in European politics, convened the Fourth Lateran Council and exercised a strong tutelage over kings and crusades.

Cencio Savelli, a camerlengo of the Church and guardian of the young Frederick II, was pope between 1216 and 1227. He approved the Dominican order (1216) and the Franciscan rule (1223), and crowned Emperor Frederick II in 1220.
Pope of strong legal and political personality, great adversary of Frederick II. His pontificate reinforced the Pontifical Inquisition and deepened the conflict between papacy and Empire.
Goffredo da Castiglione was elected in 1241 in a conclave locked up by Senator Matteo Rosso Orsini and died seventeen days later. After his death the seat became vacant almost two years.
Pope faced Frederick II in the final phase of the great conflict between papacy and empire. The Council of Lyon of 1245 declared the emperor deposed and radicalized the political struggle.
Rinaldo dei Conti di Segni, nephew of Gregory IX, was pope between 1254 and 1261. He continued the fight against the Hohenstaufen in the Kingdom of Sicily and canonized Saint Clare of Assisi in 1255.

Jacques Pantaléon, son of a shoemaker of Troyes and former Latin patriarch of Jerusalem, was pope between 1261 and 1264. He instituted the feast of Corpus Christi and offered the kingdom of Sicily to Charles of Anjou in front of Manfredo.

Guy Foulques, a Provencal jurist and advisor to Louis IX, became a widower clergyman and was pope between 1265 and 1268. He invited Charles of Anjou from the Kingdom of Sicily, who defeated Manfredo in Benevento (1266) and Conradino in Tagliacozzo (1268).
Pierre de Tarentaise, Dominican theologian and archbishop of Lyon, was the first pope of the order of preachers. He ruled the Church only a few months from 1276.
Ottobuono Fieschi, nephew of Innocent IV and legacy in England during the baron war, was elected in 1276 and died a little more than a month later, without receiving priestly ordination.

Portuguese physician and philosopher, traditionally identified with Pedro Hispano, author of the Logical Summulae, was pope since 1276. He died in 1277 when the roof of his stay in the Viterbo palace collapsed.

Giovanni Gaetano Orsini, of the great Roman family, was pope between 1277 and 1280. He obtained from Rodolfo of Habsburg the renunciation of the Romagna and favored his relatives, so Dante placed him among the simonics.

Simon de Brion, French and former chancellor of Louis IX, was pope between 1281 and 1285. He supported Charles of Anjou after the Sicilian Vespers (1282), excommunicated Peter III of Aragon and offered his kingdom to Charles of Valois, son of the king of France.
Giacomo Savelli, nephew grandson of Honorius III, was pope between 1285 and 1287. He continued to support the Angevins in the war against the Crown of Aragon for Sicily.

Girolamo Masci, the former general of the Franciscans, was the first pope of that order (1288–1292). He pushed the missions in Asia and saw Acre fall, the last cross stronghold in the Holy Land, in 1291.

Pietro da Morrone, hermit of the Abruzzo, was elected pope in 1294 after more than two years of vacant seat. He resigned at five months, and his successor Boniface VIII kept him in detention until his death in 1296.

Pope with a strong theocratic conception, faced directly with Philip IV of France. His pontificate culminated in the crisis of Anagni, symbol of the retreat of papal political power against the monarchies.

Niccolò Boccasini, master general of the Dominicans, was elected in 1303, after the death of Boniface VIII. He raised part of the sentences against Philip IV of France and died in Perugia after eight months of pontificate.
French pope whose pontificate was linked to the transfer of the pontifical court to Avignon and to the suppression of the Order of Temple under the pressure of Philip IV of France.
Pope of Avignon whose long pontificate was marked by conflicts with Louis IV of Bavaria and by a strong financial and administrative reorganization of the curia.
Jacques Fournier, Cistercian and Inquisitor in Pamiers, was pope in Avignon between 1334 and 1342. He began the construction of the palace of the Popes and reformed religious orders.

Pierre Roger, Benedictine and chancellor of Philip VI of France, was pope in Avignon between 1342 and 1352. He bought the city from Queen Joan of Naples in 1348 and expanded the palace with a lavish court.
Étienne Aubert, a Lenin jurist, was pope in Avignon between 1352 and 1362. He sent Cardinal Gil de Albornoz to recover for the Holy See the government of the Pontifical States.
Guillaume de Grimoard, Benedictine and canonist, was pope between 1362 and 1370. He returned to Rome in 1367, but returned to Avignon in 1370 and died there that same year.
Pierre Roger de Beaufort, nephew of Clement VI, was the last pope of Avignon. He moved the court to Rome in 1377, and his death the following year preceded the schism of the West.
Bartolomeo Prignano, archbishop of Bari, was elected in Rome in 1378. His hardness led the cardinals to elect Clement VII, and so began the schism of the West.
Pietro Tomacelli, a Neapolitan, was the pope of Roman obedience between 1389 and 1404, during the schism. He restored the pontifical authority in Rome and in the states of the Church.
Cosimo Migliorati was the pope of Roman obedience between 1404 and 1406. A revolt in Rome forced him to take refuge in Viterbo in 1405.
Angelo Correr, a Venetian, was the Roman pope of the schism between 1406 and 1415. He resigned before the council of Constance to allow the election of Martin V and the end of the schism.
Pope whose election at the Council of Constance ended the Great Schism of the West. His return to Rome began the political reconstruction of the Pontifical States.
Gabriele Condulmer, Venetian and nephew of Gregory XII, was pope between 1431 and 1447. He faced the Basel Council and presided over the ephemeral union with the Greek Church in Florence (1439).
A humanist pope and patron who promoted Rome’s cultural renewal. His library and artistic projects laid the groundwork for the great papal patronage of the Renaissance.
Pope humanist, diplomat and writer, formerly known as Eneas Silvio Piccolomini. He defended a renewed crusade against the Ottomans and left valuable autobiographical writings.
Pietro Barbo, a Venetian and nephew of Eugene IV, was pope between 1464 and 1471. He built the palace of St. Mark, today Palazzo Venezia, and dissolved the Roman academy of Pomponium Leto.
Renaissance Pope who strengthened the power of his family through nepotism and promoted great works in Rome. He named the Sistine Chapel and was involved in Italian politics of his time.

Giovanni Battista Cibo, Genoese, was a pope between 1484 and 1492. He published the bull against desidering Summis witchcraft (1484) and married his son Franceschetto to a daughter of Lorenzo de Medici.
Francesco Todeschini Piccolomini, nephew of Pius II, was elected in September 1503 and died twenty-six days later.

Renaissance Pope, political commander and great patrons. He promoted the reconstruction of St. Peter and commissioned decisive works to Michelangelo, Raphael and Bramante as he fought to strengthen the Pontifical States.
Pope Medici and great patrons of the Renaissance. His pontificate coincided with the beginning of Luther's Reformation and with an intense Italian and cultural policy.
Adriano de Utrecht, preceptor of Charles V and governor of Castile during the Communities, was pope between 1522 and 1523. He was the last non-Italian pope until 1978.
Pope Medici caught between Francis I and Charles V during the Italian wars. His pontificate was marked by the plunder of Rome in 1527 and by the marriage crisis of Henry VIII.
Pope Farnesio who promoted Catholic renewal and convened the Council of Trent. His pontificate was decisive in the institutionalization of the Counter-Reform.
Giovanni Maria Ciocchi del Monte, one of the presidents of the Council of Trent, was pope between 1550 and 1555. He reopened the Council in 1551 and built the Giulia village in Rome.
Marcello Cervini, a humanist and president of the Council of Trent, was pope for twenty-two days in 1555. Palestrina dedicated the Missa Papae Marcelli to him.

Gian Pietro Carafa, co-founder of the Teatines and reorganiser of the Roman Inquisition, was pope between 1555 and 1559. He created the ghetto of Rome, promulgated the first Index of Forbidden Books and confronted Philip II.

Giovanni Angelo Medici, Milanese without kinship with the Medici of Florence, was pope between 1559 and 1565. He reopened and concluded the Council of Trent (1562–1563); his nephew Carlos Borromeo led his government.
Dominican Pope and central figure of the Catholic Reformation. He promoted the application of Trento and the Holy League that defeated the Ottoman fleet in Lepanto in 1571.
Pope known above all for the reform of the calendar that bears his name. He also promoted Catholic education and the strengthening of counter-reform institutions.
Pope of brief but energetic pontificate, reorganized the administration of the curia and transformed urbanistically Rome by great works and new monumental paths.
Giovanni Battista Castagna was pope for thirteen days in 1590 and died of malaria before his coronation.
Niccolò Sfondrati, bishop of Cremona, was pope between 1590 and 1591. He supported the Catholic League against Henry of Navarre in the wars of religion of France.
Giovanni Antonio Facchinetti, Boloñés, was pope for two months in 1591.
Ippolito Aldobrandini was pope between 1592 and 1605. He absolved Henry IV of France (1595), incorporated Ferrara into the States of the Church (1598) and presided over the Jubilee of 1600.
Alessandro de' Medici, of the Florentine family, was elected in April 1605 and died 27 days later.
Camillo Borghese was pope between 1605 and 1621. He cast the doubt against Venice (1606) and finished the facade of St. Peter; his nephew Scipione Borghese gathered a large collection of art.

Alessandro Ludovisi, Boloños, was pope between 1621 and 1623. He created the Congregation of Propaganda Fide (1622), regulated the conclave with secret vote and canonized Ignatius of Loyola and Francisco Javier.
Pope Barberini during the Thirty Years' War. His pontificate combined great artistic patronage, family politics and the famous trial against Galileo.
Giovanni Battista Pamphilj was pope between 1644 and 1655. He protested against the peace of Westphalia and commissioned Bernini the source of the Four Rivers; Velázquez painted his portrait in 1650.

Fabio Chigi, Sienese and Nuncio in Münster during the Westphalia negotiations, was pope between 1655 and 1667. He commissioned Bernini the colonnade of St. Peter’s Square and received Cristina from Sweden in Rome.
Giulio Rospigliosi, librettist and diplomat, was pope between 1667 and 1669. He measured in the peace of Aachen (1668) and supported Venice in the defense of Candía.
Emilio Altieri was elected in 1670, almost eighty years old, and his adopted nephew, Cardinal Paluzzo Altieri, led the government until his death in 1676.
Pope Reformer and adversary of the ecclesiastical policy of Louis XIV. He diplomatically supported European resistance to the Ottoman advance of the late 17th century.
Pietro Ottoboni, a Venetian, was pope between 1689 and 1691. He helped Venice in the war against the Ottomans and condemned the Gallican declaration of 1682.
Marquis of Spinazzola of the Pignatelli dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.
Noble of the Carafa dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.
Noble of the Carafa dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.
Marquis de Cerchiara of the Pignatelli dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.
Noble of the Carafa dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples.
Cardinal theatino and archbishop of Naples. He was a relative of Innocent XII by a branch other than the Pignatelli, not direct nephew of the pope.
Brother of Cardinal Francesco Pignatelli. He occupied viceroyalties in Sardinia and Sicily; a viceroy administered in the name of the monarchy and was not sovereign of those territories.

Antonio Pignatelli, of the branch of Cerchiara, was pope as Innocent XII. His parents were Francesco Pignatelli of Spinazzola and Porzia Carafa; the papal career should not be confused with the Neapolitan family lordships.

Giovanni Francesco Albani was pope between 1700 and 1721. In the Spanish War of Succession he had to recognize Archduke Charles as king of Spain (1709), and condemned Jansenism with the bull Unigenitus (1713).
Michelangelo Conti, of the same family as Innocent III, was pope between 1721 and 1724.
Pietro Francesco Orsini, Dominican and Archbishop of Benevento, was pope between 1724 and 1730. He left the government in the hands of his secretary, Cardinal Niccolò Coscia.
Lorenzo Corsini, Florentine, was pope between 1730 and 1740. Blind since 1732, condemned Freemasonry in 1738 and undertook the construction of the fontana of Trevi.
Prospero Lambertini, a canonist from Bologna, was pope between 1740 and 1758. He signed with Spain and other states and corresponded with scholars of the Enlightenment.
Carlo Rezzonico, a Venetian, was pope between 1758 and 1769. He defended the Society of Jesus against his expulsion from Portugal, France, Spain and Naples.
Lorenzo Ganganelli, Franciscan Conventual, was pope between 1769 and 1774. Pressed by the Bourbons, he abolished the Society of Jesus in 1773.
Pope between 1775 and 1799. He faced the ecclesiastical reforms of Joseph II and the French Revolution; French troops occupied Rome and died prisoner in Valence.
Notary of the Da Vinci dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Artist, engineer and researcher of the Renaissance. He worked for different Italian courts and ended his days in France under the protection of Francis I.
Noble of the Gherardini dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Mercader of the dynasty of the Giocondo. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
De facto ruler of Florence and great patrons of the Renaissance. Under his leadership, the Medici consolidated their political and cultural influence in the Italy of the Quattrocento.
Consort of the Orsini dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence, Rome.
Brother of Pope Leo X, he ruled Florence after the return of the Medici in 1512 and was Duke of Nemours. His tomb, the work of Michelangelo, is in the New Sacristy of St. Lawrence.
Ruler of Florence, 1502–1512. Ruler of the Soderini dynasty.
Governor of the Amboise dynasty. His career is linked to France, Milan.
Artist of the Melzi dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan, France.
Duchess of the Ávalos dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Naples, Ischia.

He inherited Roberto's Naples and faced a crisis after the murder of her husband Andrés de Anjou. The invasions of Louis of Hungary, the power of her second husband Louis of Taranto and his election of Louis de Anjou as heir turned the Neapolitan succession into a European conflict.
Prince of the Borja dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples, Squillace.
Consort of the Trastámara dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples, Squillace.

people.nombre: Alfonso of Aragon, Duke of Bisceglie
people.resumen: Duke of the Trastámara dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples, Bisceglie.
Noble of the Borja dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples, Bisceglie.
Noble of the Sforza dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan.

people.nombre: Charles VI of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: Emperor Habsburg and rival of Philip V in the War of Succession. His house ruled Milan, Naples and Sardinia on different dates; he exchanged Sardinia for Sicily in 1720. The Pragmatic Sanction sought to secure his inheritance to Mary Theresa.

people.nombre: Francis I of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: Duke of Lorraine and then Grand Duke of Tuscany, he became emperor by his marriage to Mary Theresa. His union founded the house of Habsburg-Lorraine.
Consort of the Bourbon dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Spain, Tuscany, Holy Roman Empire.

people.nombre: Leopold II of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: Emperor Habsburg of brief reign, succeeded after governing Tuscany. He moderated several reforms by Joseph II and faced the expansion of the French Revolution in Europe.

people.nombre: Francis II of the Holy Roman Empire
people.resumen: Last emperor of the Holy Roman Empire and first emperor of Austria since 1804. He fought revolutionary and Napoleonic France, dissolved the Empire in 1806 and married his daughter Mary Louise to Napoleon.

Inigo López de Loyola, born in a family of the small Basque nobility, changed his life after being wounded in the defense of Pamplona in 1521. His spiritual experience gave rise to the Exercises. In Paris he brought together the companions of the future Society of Jesus, approved by Paul III in 1540, of which he was the first Superior General.
Cardinal. His trajectory is linked to Pontifical States.
Theologian. His trajectory is linked to Spain, Pontifical States.
Theologian. His trajectory is linked to Spain, Pontifical States.
Cardinal. His trajectory is linked to Milan, Pontifical States.
Cardinal of the Orsini dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Pontifical States.
Cardinal of the Colonna dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Pontifical States.
Cardinal of the Riario dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Pontifical States.
Lord of the Della Rovere dynasty, your trajectory is linked to Pontifical States.
Consort of the Montefeltro dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Pontifical States.
Duke of Urbino, 1508–1516. Duke of Urbino of the Della Rovere dynasty.
Governor of Florence, 1464–1469. Lord of the Medici dynasty.
Noble of the Tornabuoni dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Noble of the Medici dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Noble of the Gorini dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Duke of Parma, 1545–1547. Duke of the Farnesian dynasty.
Consort of the Orsini dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Parma.
Jurist of the Aldobrandini dynasty. His career is linked to Florence, Rome.
Cardinal of the Aldobrandini dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Papal States.
Cardinal of the Borghese dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Pontifical States.
Trader of the Barberini dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Noble of the Barbadori dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence, Rome.

Nephew of Urban VIII and brother of Taddeo and Antonio, Francesco Barberini was created cardinal in 1623. He performed diplomatic and governmental functions and gathered an important library of manuscripts. After the election of Innocent X he took refuge in France in 1646; he returned later to Rome, where he died in 1679.

The son of Carlo Barberini and Costanza Magalotti, he was one of Urban VIII's cardinal nephews: his appointment, reserved since 1627, became public in 1628. He shared with his brothers Francesco and Taddeo the power and patronage of the family and, after 1644, the difficulties with Innocent X. He distinguished himself from his uncle, the Capuchin Cardinal of the same name.
Cardinal of the Chigi dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Pontifical States.
Noble of the Cusani dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan.
Diplomat, civil servant and Florentine writer whose political experience was fed by The Prince and the Discourses. He closely observed Caesar Borja and the Italian powers of the early 16th century.
Governor of Florence, 1492–1494. Lord of the Medici dynasty.
Noble of the Orsini dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence, Rome.
The nephew of Pope Leo X, he ruled Florence and was appointed Duke of Urbino in 1516. Machiavelli dedicated The Prince to him; he was the father of Catherine of Medici.
Consort of the Auvergne dynasty. His career is linked to France, Florence.
Consort of the Hohenstaufen dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Sicily, Thuringia.
Last Hohenstaufen, grandson of Frederick II. At sixteen years old he tried to recover Sicily from Charles of Anjou; defeated in Tagliacozzo (1268), he was beheaded in Naples.
He consolidated the Savoy domains on both sides of the Alps after a difficult minority. His offspring opened roads to the English and Provencal courts and to the Italian lordships.
Consort of the Geneva Dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Savoy, Geneva.
He succeeded Thomas I and had to negotiate with his brothers the distribution of family rights. His Italian policy brought him closer to Frederick II.
Consort of the Burgundy dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Savoy, Burgundy.
Consort of the Baux dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Savoy, Provence.
Count of Savoy, 1253–1263. Count of the Savoy dynasty.

Before inheriting the county, he developed an important career in England and gathered his own domains around Lake Leman. His government strengthened controls over Castilians, income and administration.
He abandoned his ecclesiastical career before succeeding his brother Peter II. Without his own offspring, he had to prepare an inheritance in which the sons and grandsons of Thomas II competed.
Brother of Amadeus IV, he received rights in Piedmont and ruled Flanders for his marriage to Joan. He was not the successor of his father in Savoy County.
Consort of the Fieschi dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Piedmont, Savoy.

Son of Thomas II, he entered the county after the death of his uncle Philip I. His position was consolidated by agreements with other branches of the family, which retained their own rights. Edward and Aimon succeeded in Savoy; by their marriages, the count also linked with Bâgé and Brabant.
Consort of the Bâgé dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Savoy.
Count of Savoy, 1323–1329. Count of Savoy dynasty.

Amadeus V's youngest son, inherited after his brother Edward, whose daughter also defended inheritance rights. His marriage to Yolanda de Monferrato united the Savoy with the new Italian branch of the Paleologists.
The daughter of Theodore I of Monferrato, she married Aimon of Savoy. Her ancestry was linked to Emperor Andronic II and to the Alleramic heiress Yolanda, named Irene in Byzantium.

Known as the Green Count, he belongs to the generation that reinforced Savoy’s political and military projection. He was the son of Aimon and Yolanda of Monferrato, so his ancestry brings together Savoy and Paleologists.
Consort of the Bourbon dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Bourbon, Savoy.

The Red Count succeeded his father Amadeus VI and maintained the relationship with the French monarchy. He married Bona of Berry and was the father of Amadeus VIII. His early death left a child heir and opened a struggle for the regency between the mother and grandmother of the new Count.
Consort of the Valois dynasty. His trajectory is linked to France, Savoy.
He inherited as a child and became the first Duke of Savoy in 1416. The elevation of rank did not create a new dynasty.
Consort of the Valois-Borgoña dynasty. His career is linked to Burgundy, Savoy.
Son of Amadeus VIII and Maria of Burgundy, he assumed government functions before becoming Duke. His marriage to Anna of Lusignan linked Savoy to Cyprus.

Daughter of King Janus of Cyprus, he married Louis of Savoy and brought to the Alpine court a direct connection with the Lusignans. His numerous offspring linked with France, Milan and the Cypriot succession itself.
Duke of Savoy since 1465, of fragile health by epilepsy. His wife Yolanda of France ruled in practice. He was beatified by his piety.
Consort of the Valois dynasty. His trajectory is linked to France, Savoy.
Duke of Savoy, 1472–1482. Duke of Savoy Dynasty.

He inherited the duchy of his brother Filiberto I. His marriage to Blanche of Montferrat reinforced Savoy's expectations of the Palaeologists' heritage, while the intervention in Saluzzo confronted him with French interests.

The son of Louis and Anna of Cyprus, he came to the duchy by extinguishing the male offspring of his brother Amadeus IX. His brief government preceded those of his sons Filiberto II and Charles III, born of different marriages.
Consort of the Bourbon dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Bourbon, Savoy.
Consort of the Brosse dynasty, his trajectory is linked to Savoy.
He inherited from his father Philip II and married Margaret of Austria. The link brought Savoy closer to the Habsburgs and the Netherlands.
Duke of Savoy between 1504 and 1553. In 1536 France occupied almost all its states and Geneva consolidated its independence; their son Manuel Filiberto recovered them in 1559.
Consort of the Avis dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Portugal, Savoy.

He inherited a duchy largely occupied by other powers. His service to Charles V and Philip II, and especially the victory of San Quintin, contributed to the territorial recovery agreed upon at Cateau-Cambresis.
Consort of the Valois-Angulema dynasty. His career is linked to France, Savoy.
The son of Manuel Filiberto, he ruled in a scenario dominated by rivalries between France and the Spanish Monarchy. His marriage to Catherine Micaela connected him to Philip II.

The daughter of Philip II and Elizabeth of Valois, he married Charles Manuel I of Savoy. His marriage placed the descendants of the Duke within the family network of the Habsburgs and the Valois. Among his sons were Victor Amadeus I and Thomas Francis, for whom he continued the branch of Carignano.

A younger son of Charles Emmanuel I and Catherine Michelle, he began the branch of Savoy-Carignano. He married Marie de Bourbon-Soissons and participated in the disputes against the regency of Christine of France.
Princess of Carignano of the Bourbon-Condé dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to France, Savoy.

Son of Thomas Francis of Savoy-Carignano, he inherited from his mother the county of Soissons and served as a general in the armies of Louis XIV. He married Olympia Mancini, niece of Mazarino, and was the father of Prince Eugene.

The nephew of Cardinal Mazarino, a prominent figure of the court of Louis XIV and wife of Eugenio Maurice de Savoy, Count of Soissons. Involved in the "case of poisons", she fled France in 1680 and lived in the Spanish Netherlands; she was the mother of Prince Eugene.

Prince of the house of Savoy-Carignano raised in the court of Louis XIV, passed in 1683 to the service of the Habsburgs and became the great general of the Empire. He defeated the Ottomans in Zenta (1697) and Belgrade (1717) and, together with Marlborough, to France in Blenheim, Oudenarde and Malplaquet during the Spanish War of Succession.
Duke of Savoy, 1638–1675. Duke of Savoy Dynasty.
Consort of the Savoy-Nemours dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Savoy, France.
King of Sardinia and Duke of Savoy who continued the territorial expansion of his dynasty in northern Italy. He actively participated in the great European wars of the eighteenth century.
Consort of the Hesse dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Hesse, Savoy.
King of Sardinia and Duke of Savoy since 1773. The war with revolutionary France cost Savoy and Nice, ceded by the armistice of Cherasco in 1796.
Consort of the Bourbon dynasty. His career is linked to Spain, Savoy.
King of Sardinia since 1796. French troops forced him to leave their continental states in 1798; he took refuge in Sardinia and abdicated in his brother Victor Manuel I in 1802.
Consort of the Bourbon dynasty. His trajectory is linked to France, Savoy.
King of Sardinia since 1802. He recovered Piedmont and Savoy in 1814 and obtained Genoa at the Congress of Vienna; abdicated in 1821 after the liberal Piedmontese revolution.
King of Sardinia between 1821 and 1831, brother of Victor Manuel I. He restored an absolutist government after the revolution of 1821 and was the last of the main line of Savoy.
The son of Thomas Francis and Mary of Bourbon-Soissons, continued the branch of Carignano. Her marriage to Angela Caterina of East added an Italian connection to the Savoyard and Bourbon heritage.
Princess of Carignano of the East Dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Modena, Savoy.
Prince of Carignano of the Savoy-Carignan dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Savoy, Piedmont.
Princess of Carignano of the Savoy dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Savoy.
Prince of Carignano of the Savoy-Carignan dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Savoy, Piedmont.
Princess of Carignano of the Hesse dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Hesse, Savoy.
Prince of Carignano of the Savoy-Carignan dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Savoy, Piedmont.
Princess of Carignano of the Lorraine dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Lorraine, Savoy.
Prince of Carignano of the Savoy-Carignan dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Savoy, Piedmont.
Princess of Carignan of the Wettin Dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Saxony, Savoy.
King of Sardinia since 1831, of the Savoy-Carignano branch. He granted the Statute of 1848 and declared war on Austria; defeated in Novara (1849), abdicated in Victor Manuel II.
Banker of the Medici dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Noble of the Bueri dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Banker and political leader who established the supremacy of the Medici in the 15th century Florence. His patronage laid the cultural and financial foundations of family power.
Noble of the Bardi dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Banker of the Medici dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Noble of the Cavalcanti dynasty. Its trajectory is linked to Florence.
Banker of the Medici dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Noble of the Acciaiuoli dynasty. Its trajectory is linked to Florence.
Political of the Medici dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Noble of the Medici dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Political of the Salviati dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Noble of the Salviati dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Cardinal of the Medici dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence, Papal States.
First Duke of Florence (1532), imposed with the support of Charles V, whose natural daughter Margaret married him. He was murdered in 1537 by his cousin Lorenzino de Medici.
Grand Duke of Tuscany between 1609 and 1621. He protected Galileo Galilei, who in 1610 baptized the moons of Jupiter in his honor as "medicean stars".
Consort of the Habsburg dynasty. His career is linked to Austria, Tuscany.
Grand Duke of Tuscany between 1621 and 1670. He faced the plague of 1630, protected Galileo and with his brother Leopoldo promoted the Accademia del Cimento.
Consort of the Della Rovere dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Urbino, Tuscany.
Grand Duke of Tuscany between 1670 and 1723, the longest reign of the dynasty. His government coincided with the economic stagnation of the state and the succession crisis of the Medici.
Consort of the Bourbon-Orleans-Gaston dynasty. His trajectory is linked to France, Tuscany.
Electress consort of the Medici dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Tuscany, Palatinate.
Grand Duke of Tuscany, 1723–1737. Grand Duke of the Medici dynasty.
Consort of the Valois dynasty. His trajectory is linked to France, Naples.
Duke of Durazzo, 1336–1348. Duke of the Anjou-Durazzo dynasty.
Noble of the Baux dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples, Provence.
Noble of the Montefeltro dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Urbino, Rome.
Consort of the Colonna dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Urbino, Rome.
Princess of the Avis dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Portugal, Parma.
Consort of the Brabant dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Brabant, Savoy.
Daughter of Amadeus V of Savoy and wife of Andronicus III Paleologist. He was regent by his son John V during the civil war against John Cantacuceno (1341–1347).
Notary of the Medici dynasty of Milan. His trajectory is linked to Milan.
Noble of the Serbian dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Milan.
Noble of the Salviati dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Noble of the Medici dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Noble of the Brandano dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence, Urbino.
Noble of the Deti dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Florence.
Duchess of the East Dynasty. Her trajectory is linked to Ferrara, France, Guisa.
Duke of the Colonna dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Naples, Pontifical States.
Noble of the Trastámara-Naples dynasty. Its trajectory is linked to Naples, Pontifical States.
Roman noble and admiral at the service of the Hispanic Monarchy and the papacy. He sent one of the great wings of the fleet of the Holy League in the battle of Lepanto.
Venetian Admiral who led the Venice contingent in Lepanto and later was elected Dux. He represented the decisive weight of the republic in the naval war against the Ottomans.
Genoese Admiral at the service of the Hispanic Monarchy and heir to the naval tradition of Andrea Doria. He participated as commander in the Christian fleet of Lepanto.
Admiral of the Barbarigo dynasty, his trajectory is linked to Venice.
Spanish Admiral and Marquis of Santa Cruz, one of the great naval commanders of the 16th century. He participated in the Mediterranean strategy of Philip II and in the conquest of Portugal.
Spanish general who transformed the Italian war by a flexible combination of infantry, fortification and artillery. His victories consolidated Spanish dominance over Naples.
Count of Jaffa and Ashkelon of the Aleramici dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Monferrato, Jerusalem.
Marquis of Montferrato who defended Tyre in front of Saladin in 1187. Married to Elizabeth I of Jerusalem and elected king in 1192, he was killed days later.
Queen of Jerusalem since her birth in 1212, daughter of John of Brienne and Mary of Montferrato. Married in 1225 to Emperor Frederick II, she died when she gave birth to Conrad in 1228.
Consort of the Dandolo dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Venice, Serbia.
Duke of Parma, 1622–1646. Duke of the Farnesian dynasty.
Duke of Parma, 1646–1694. Duke of the Farnesian dynasty.
Crown prince of the Farnesian dynasty, his trajectory is linked to Parma.
Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Palatinate, Parma.
Duke of Mantua, 1612–1612. Duke of the Gonzaga dynasty.
Duke of Mantua, 1612–1626. Duke of the Gonzaga dynasty.
Duke of Mantua, 1626–1627. Duke of the Gonzaga dynasty.
Marquess of the East Dynasty. His trajectory is linked to Modena.
Duke of Modena, 1597–1628. Duke of the East Dynasty.
Duke of Modena, 1628–1629. Duke of the East Dynasty.
Duke of Modena, 1629–1658. Duke of the East Dynasty.
He succeeded Peter II during his childhood. Rivalries between Baronial families and Neapolitan pressure weakened the kingdom; his death during an epidemic left the crown to his brother Frederick.

He inherited the kingdom as a minor and was subjected to the struggles of the great lords. His marriage to Martin the Younger and the expedition of 1392 restored the royal power with Aragonese support, without erasing the identity of the island crown.

Husband of Mary of Sicily and son of Martin the Human. He reorganized the power of the island monarchy in front of the barons and died after a campaign in Sardinia. His death without a legitimate surviving heir aggravated the succession of the Crown of Aragon.

Second husband of Joan I of Naples, he tried to impose his authority on the government of the kingdom. His shared reign coincided with the Hungarian invasions and the search for legitimacy following the murder of Andrew of Anjou.

He inherited the crown of Charles III during the minority age and disputed the kingdom to Louis II of Anjou. His mother Margaret's regency ensured the continuity of the house of Durazzo; later extended his intervention to the politics of Rome.

The daughter of Bernabò Visconti, she married Peter II to strengthen relations between Milan and Cyprus. Her only daughter died a little. After widowing she returned to Italy; she should not be confused with Valentina Visconti, Duchess of Orleans.

people.nombre: Louis of Savoy, King of Cyprus
people.resumen: The son of Louis of Savoy and Anna of Cyprus, he married his cousin Carlota. His royal dignity came from that marriage and was then reduced to a pretense in exile. It should not be confused with his father, Duke of Savoy.

Noble Venetian married to James II, exercised regency during the brief life of his son and continued as queen after his death. The pressure of Venice ended with his abdication in 1489. His retirement in Asolo maintained a remarkable cultural projection.

people.nombre: Gaston of Foix, Duke of Nemours
people.resumen: The son of John of Foix and Mary of Orleans, he was nephew of Louis XII and brother of Germana of Foix. He led French forces during the wars of Italy and died in the Battle of Ravenna in 1512. His career brings together the Pyrenean connections of the Foix and military service to the French monarchy.
The daughter of John James of Monferrato and Joan of Savoy, he married Ludovico I of Saluzzo. His son Ludovico II thus gathered ancestry from the Saluzzo, the Italian Paleologists and the Savoy.

The daughter of William VIII of Monferrato, he married Charles I of Savoy. After the death of the Duke he assumed the regency for his son Carlos Juan Amadeo and defended his authority before the relatives of the house.
The son of Charles I and Blanche of Montferrat, Savoy inherited before his first birthday. His mother exercised the regency.
The son of Juan Jacobo and Juana de Savoy combined the government of Monferrato with the military service of the Italian powers. His daughters married Ludovico II of Saluzzo and Charles I of Savoy.
Son of Theodore II, Monferrato inherited and married Joan of Savoy, sister of Amadeus VIII. The kinship did not prevent the pressure of the saboyan duke on his domains.

people.nombre: Joanna of Savoy, Marchioness of Montferrat
people.resumen: The daughter of Amadeus VII and Bona of Berry, she married John James of Monferrato. She was the mother of William VIII, Bonifacio III and Isabel, wife of Ludovico I of Saluzzo.
Son of John II and Isabella of Mallorca, Monferrato inherited after his brother John III. His government was crossed by relations with Milan and by disputes with Savoy-Acaya.
One of the main aleramic marquises, he extended his influence to cities in northern Italy. His daughter Yolanda married Andronic II and took the name Irene.
Born as Yolanda, daughter of William VII, she adopted Irene's name when she married Andronic II Paleologist. Monferrato was linked to the Byzantine imperial court.

Son of Andronico II and Irene of Monferrato, he passed from the Byzantine imperial family to the government of an Italian marquisate. His rights came from his mother, but he had to defend them against competitors.

The son of Juan Jacobo, succeeded his brother William VIII when expectations of Monferrato’s inheritance already affected Savoy and Saluzzo. His sons William IX and John George extended the male line of the Paleologists.

He inherited Monferrato de Boniface III and married Anne of Alençon. Her children Margarita and Bonifacio would occupy different positions in the succession: he inherited the marquisate; she transmitted the rights that would end up holding his incorporation into the heritage of Gonzaga.

Wife of William IX, he exercised the tutelage of his son Bonifacio IV and defended the interests of the Paleologists during the Italian wars. He also intervened in the marriage negotiations that ended up uniting his daughter Margarita with Frederick II Gonzaga.
The son of William IX and Anne of Alençon, Monferrato inherited at the age of six, under guardianship. He died young and without offspring, so his uncle Juan Jorge succeeded him.
Son of Boniface III and brother of William IX, he succeeded his nephew Boniface IV. He was the last Marquis of the legitimate male line of the Paleologists.

Grand Duke of Tuscany, 1790–1799. Grand Duke of the Habsburg-Lorraine dynasty.

Barnabas Chiaramonti, Benedictine born in Cesena in 1742, was elected in Venice in 1800. He signed the concordat with Napoleon (1801), attended his coronation (1804) and was his prisoner between 1809 and 1814; he died in 1823.
Lord of Milan, 1339–1349 (corregent). Lord of the Visconti dynasty.
Lord of Milan, 1339–1354 (corregent). Lord of the Visconti dynasty.
Dogo de Genoa, 1339–1344. Dogo.
King of Naples, 1414–1435. King of the Anjou-Durazzo dynasty.

Noble and military in the service of the Gonzaga of Mantua, father of Baldassare Castiglione and husband of Luigia Gonzaga. He died in 1499 after the wounds suffered in Fornovo. The card does not assign a year of birth without sufficient source.

Also called Aloisa Gonzaga, she was the wife of Cristoforo Castiglione and the mother of Baldassare. She participated in the decisions of his formation and corresponded with him. Her life dates are not completed from conjecture.
Wife of Baldassare Castiglione since 1516. Her death in 1520 preceded the ecclesiastical stage and the Spanish nunciature of her husband.

Writer, humanist and diplomat of the court of Urbino, author of El cortano, published in 1528. He served Gonzaga and the Dukes of Urbino and was nuncio of Clement VII to Charles V. He died in Toledo in 1529.

Diplomat of Italian origin, cardinal and chief minister during the regency of Anne of Austria and the youth of Louis XIV. Overcame the Fronda and intervened in the negotiations of Westphalia and peace of the Pyrenees.

She was born in Venice and trained in the French court. She composed poetry and political and moral treatises, and defended the intellectual capacity and dignity of women in The City of Ladies, written in 1405.

persona.resumen: Count of Anjou who married in 1129 to Melisenda, heir of Jerusalem, and reigned with her since 1131. His son Godofredo Plantagenet was the father of Henry II of England.

gobiernos.nota: Shared authority; is not interpreted as exclusive succession.

persona.resumen: Queen of Jerusalem since 1131, daughter of Baldwin II. She ruled with Fulco and then with her son Balduino III, until he took power in 1152. She was a great religious promoter.
King of Jerusalem since 1143, son of Fulchus and Melisenda. He took power over his mother in 1152 and conquered Ashkelon in 1153.
King of Jerusalem since 1163. He tried several times to conquer Fatimid Egypt; his death in 1174 coincided with the rise of Saladin.
King of Jerusalem from the age of thirteen. Despite suffering leprosy, he personally led the kingdom and his army during the growing confrontation with Saladin.
Son of Sibilah of Jerusalem, crowned a child with his uncle Baldwin IV. He died in 1186 at barely nine years old, opening up the succession crisis that preceded the fall of Jerusalem.
Queen of Jerusalem since 1186, sister of Baldwin IV. She crowned her husband Guido of Lusignan, under whose reign Jerusalem was lost to Saladin in 1187.
Husband of Sibila and king of Jerusalem during Hattin’s defeat. After losing the capital, he continued the struggle and ended up establishing Lusignan power in Cyprus.
Marquis of Montferrato who defended Tyre in front of Saladin in 1187. Married to Elizabeth I of Jerusalem and elected king in 1192, he was killed days later.
Husband of Sibila and king of Jerusalem during Hattin’s defeat. After losing the capital, he continued the struggle and ended up establishing Lusignan power in Cyprus.

Count of Champagne, he married Isabella I of Jerusalem during the Crusades. His career brought the French comital house to the government of the Latin kingdom. His daughter Alice later married Hugh I of Cyprus, extending this family network’s presence in the eastern Mediterranean.
Queen of Jerusalem since 1190, daughter of Amalaric I. Her successive husbands, Conrad of Montferrato, Henry of Champagne and Amalarch of Lusignan, ruled the kingdom with her.
Lord of Cyprus after his brother Guido and first king of the island in 1197. That same year he married Elizabeth I and was king of Jerusalem until his death in 1205.
Byzantine Emperor since 1195 after overthrowing and blinding his brother Isaac II. He fled Constantinople at the arrival of the fourth crusade in 1203.
Lord of Cyprus after his brother Guido and first king of the island in 1197. That same year he married Elizabeth I and was king of Jerusalem until his death in 1205.
Lord of Cyprus after his brother Guido and first king of the island in 1197. That same year he married Elizabeth I and was king of Jerusalem until his death in 1205.
Queen of Jerusalem since 1205, daughter of Elizabeth I and Conrad of Montferrato. She married John of Brienne and died shortly after giving birth to Elizabeth II.
King of Cyprus since 1205, son of Amalaric of Lusignan. He participated in the fifth crusade and died in Tripoli in 1218.

gobiernos.nota: Conventional Proclamation1205; formal coronation1208. The tab represents Nicaea and its domains, without receiving the Latin states or Epirus.

persona.resumen: Founder of the empire of Nicaea after the fall of Constantinople into the hands of the fourth crusade (1204). Coronated emperor in 1208, he consolidated the main Byzantine state in exile.
French knight who became king of Jerusalem by his marriage to Mary of Montferrato in 1210. He led the fifth crusade in Damieta and was later co-regent of the Latin Empire of Constantinople.
Queen of Jerusalem since her birth in 1212, daughter of John of Brienne and Mary of Montferrato. Married in 1225 to Emperor Frederick II, she died when she gave birth to Conrad in 1228.

Daughter of Henry II of Champagne and Elizabeth of Jerusalem, he married Hugo I of Cyprus. He exercised regency functions and maintained rights and interests linked to both shores of the Mediterranean. His file connects the house of Champagne with Cyprus and Jerusalem, without reducing it to its later Navarre branch.

He agreed to the throne as a child and his minority opened the struggle between the Ibelin and Frederick II. Resistance to imperial intervention consolidated a Cypriot monarchy with a nobility capable of conditioning the government.
Latin Emperor of Constantinople since 1221, from the house of Courtenay. He lost much of his territory to Nicaea and Epirus.
Emperor of Nicea since 1221. He expanded the status of Nicen in Asia Minor and the Balkans and prepared for the recovery of Constantinople. The Orthodox Church venerates him as saint.

persona.nombre: Frederick II of the Holy Roman Empire
persona.resumen: Emperor Hohenstaufen, king of Sicily and Jerusalem, an exceptional figure of the Mediterranean policy of the thirteenth century. His conflict with the papacy and his Sicilian court marked an entire epoch.
He inherited the rights of the Hohenstaufen in Germany and Sicily in full struggle with the papacy. His death left Conrado, known as Conradino, as heir to a threatened cause.
He was the last Latin emperor to rule Constantinople. After the recovery of the city by the Byzantines, he sought in the West support to restore an empire that he only retained as a title.
French knight who became king of Jerusalem by his marriage to Mary of Montferrato in 1210. He led the fifth crusade in Damieta and was later co-regent of the Latin Empire of Constantinople.

Daughter of Henry II of Champagne and Elizabeth of Jerusalem, he married Hugo I of Cyprus. He exercised regency functions and maintained rights and interests linked to both shores of the Mediterranean. His file connects the house of Champagne with Cyprus and Jerusalem, without reducing it to its later Navarre branch.

Daughter of Bohemundo V and wife of Henry I of Cyprus, he exercised the regency of the island by his son Hugo II. His presence in Acre shows how Antioch's family alliances also influenced the politics of Jerusalem.

His reign passed under regencies and ended without descent. The succession passed to Hugo III, grandson of Hugo I by female line and son of Henry of Antioch: the surname Lusignan continued in a new family branch.
Emperor of Nicaea between 1254 and 1258, son of John III Vatatzés. Erudite and author of theological works, he died young leaving a younger son, John IV.
Last Hohenstaufen, grandson of Frederick II. At sixteen years old he tried to recover Sicily from Charles of Anjou; defeated in Tagliacozzo (1268), he was beheaded in Naples.
Emperor boy of Nicaea since 1258. Michael VIII Paleologist, his co-regent, removed him after regaining Constantinople in 1261 and ordered blinding him.

gobiernos.nota: Minor Emperor with Michael VIII; not independent authority over another empire.

persona.resumen: Emperor boy of Nicaea since 1258. Michael VIII Paleologist, his co-regent, removed him after regaining Constantinople in 1261 and ordered blinding him.

He regained Constantinople in 1261 and founded the last Byzantine imperial dynasty. He combined diplomacy and military intervention to contain Charles of Anjou; the marriages of his sons linked his house with the powers of the Black Sea.

He succeeded Hugo II along the line of Elizabeth of Cyprus, his mother, and inaugurated the branch of Antioch-Lusignan. He tried to strengthen the royal authority in Acre, but he clashed with the autonomy of the Barons and with the Angevin claims over Jerusalem.

He succeeded Hugo II along the line of Elizabeth of Cyprus, his mother, and inaugurated the branch of Antioch-Lusignan. He tried to strengthen the royal authority in Acre, but he clashed with the autonomy of the Barons and with the Angevin claims over Jerusalem.
Son of Baldwin II, last Latin emperor of Constantinople. After the Byzantine reconquest of 1261 he inherited only the title and married Beatrice, daughter of Charles of Anjou.

He reduced the military resources of the Byzantine Empire in a context of serious fiscal difficulties. The arrival of the Catalan Company and the war with his grandson Andronic III aggravated the crisis.
Son of Hugo III, king of Cyprus and titular of Jerusalem since 1284. He died in 1285 after a year of reign and succeeded him by his brother Henry II.
Son of Hugo III, king of Cyprus and titular of Jerusalem since 1284. He died in 1285 after a year of reign and succeeded him by his brother Henry II.
Last king of Jerusalem who ruled from Acre. After the fall of the city in 1291 he retained the title of Jerusalem while continuing as king of Cyprus.
Last king of Jerusalem who ruled from Acre. After the fall of the city in 1291 he retained the title of Jerusalem while continuing as king of Cyprus.
Last king of Jerusalem who ruled from Acre. After the fall of the city in 1291 he retained the title of Jerusalem while continuing as king of Cyprus.
Son of Andronicus II, associated with the throne as co-emperor. He led campaigns against the Turks and the Catalan Company without success, and died before his father in 1320.

gobiernos.nota: Away from the government by Amalarico and captive in Armenia.

persona.resumen: Last king of Jerusalem who ruled from Acre. After the fall of the city in 1291 he retained the title of Jerusalem while continuing as king of Cyprus.

persona.nombre: Amalric of Lusignan, Lord of Tyre
persona.resumen: Brother of Henry II, he removed him from the government of Cyprus and exercised the administration of the island. His marriage to Isabella of Armenia connected the Lusignans with the succession of sackcloth. He was murdered, which allowed Henry to return.

The daughter of Charles of Valois and Catherine of Courtenay, inherited the title of Latin Empress of Constantinople, already without territory. Married to Philip of Tarento, she resided in the Angevin court of Naples.
Last king of Jerusalem who ruled from Acre. After the fall of the city in 1291 he retained the title of Jerusalem while continuing as king of Cyprus.

He succeeded his uncle Henry II and established a new Lusignan branch. His marriage alliances brought the island closer to Bourbon and Aragon. He abdicated in favour of Peter I while retaining the titular dignity of Jerusalem.

He succeeded his uncle Henry II and established a new Lusignan branch. His marriage alliances brought the island closer to Bourbon and Aragon. He abdicated in favour of Peter I while retaining the titular dignity of Jerusalem.
Byzantine Emperor since 1328 after a civil war against his grandfather Andronic II. He lost almost all of Asia Minor to the Ottomans, but recovered Thessaly and Epirus.
Daughter of Amadeus V of Savoy and wife of Andronicus III Paleologist. He was regent by his son John V during the civil war against John Cantacuceno (1341–1347).
Byzantine emperor during half a century of civil wars, first against John VI Cantacuceno and then before his son Andronic IV. His empire was reduced and taxed by the Ottomans.

He promoted expeditions against the Muslim powers of the Eastern Mediterranean and sought support in the European courts. The seizure and plundering of Alexandria in 1365 did not result in a lasting conquest. His assassination opened up a crisis within the Cypriot court.

gobiernos.nota: Dynastic title without territorial domain of Jerusalem.

persona.nombre: John of Lusignan, Regent of Cyprus
persona.resumen: Brother of Peter I, he ruled during the minority of Peter II. The accusations and revenges that followed the assassination of the king confronted the members of the court. His title of prince of Antioch was nominal, as the principality had disappeared.

He inherited the crown as a minor after the murder of his father. The war with Genoa ended with the loss of Famagusta and burdensome obligations for the monarchy. He died without surviving offspring, so that his uncle James succeeded him.

gobiernos.nota: Title of the Neapolitan monarchy, without effective rule in the Holy Land.

persona.resumen: Charles of Durazzo ruled Croatia and Dalmatia by delegation of Louis I before conquering Naples in 1381. His domains included Corfu and Butrinto; his authority over Achaia was nominal, in front of the local power of the Navarra Company. Coronado king of Hungary and Croatia on 31 December 1385, suffered an attack on Buddha in February 1386 and died shortly after. His title of Jerusalem did not imply control of the Holy Land.

gobiernos.nota: Chosen during his captivity in Genoa.

persona.resumen: He was elected king while he remained captive in Genoa. His release and return demanded concessions that maintained the commercial dependence of the island. After the death of Leon V he incorporated into his title the nominal crown of Armenia.

Byzantine Emperor since 1391. Traveled through Western Europe seeking help against the Ottomans; Bayezid's defeat to Tamerlan in 1402 gave Constantinople a break.

Born during the captivity of his parents in Genoa, he attempted to recover margin from the Genoese. The Mamluk invasion of 1426 ended with his capture and imposition of tribute. His sons connected the island with Savoy and continued the dynasty.

The penultimate Byzantine emperor (1425–1448) sought Western help against the Ottomans and accepted the union of the Churches at the Council of Florence (1439).

He ruled an island subject to Mamluk tribute and with Famagusta in genoese hands. His court welcomed Greek influences reinforced by his marriage to Helena Paleologian. His sons Carlota and James then disputed the succession.

Last Byzantine emperor. He died defending Constantinople during the siege of 1453, and his death was associated with the end of the Roman Empire of the East.

He inherited the crown of John II and defended it in front of his half brother James. After losing his last bastion he went into exile and maintained his dynastic rights, which would end up linked to Savoy. His effective government is distinguished from his subsequent claim.
