persona.resumen: He disputed the heritage of the united monarchy, but eventually recognized the separation of Kajetia and Imereti. His kingdom was centered on Kartli. His sons gave continuity to the royal line and the princely branch of Mukhrani.

The rivalry with Kajetia and the safavid expansion conditioned his reign. He temporarily incorporated the neighboring kingdom, which later regained its autonomy. His abdication left the crown first to his brother and then to his son Luarsab.

Brother of David X, he assumed the crown after his abdication and gave it to his nephew Luarsab. His brief government links two generations of the Bagrationi in a period of increasing Persian intervention.

Poet and king, alternated resistance, negotiation and exile in the face of pressure from Abbas I and his successors. The rebellion of 1625 allowed him to return and extend his authority to Kartli, but Rostom ended up moving him. His family suffered captivity, executions and displacement.

The daughter of George X of Kartli and wife of Teimuraz I of Kajetia. The marriage strengthened the cooperation between the two branches during their wars against Persia. Their children linked this generation with the later kings of Kajetia and Imereti.

He spent part of his youth in Russia and ended up accepting the saphavid investiture. He ruled Kartli and later received the crown of Kajetia, administered locally by his son David. His trajectory connects the Bagrationi exiles with the service to the sah.

He received the kajetia crown in the context of the safavid collapse and briefly occupied Tbilisi in front of Vajtang VI. Ottoman intervention altered his alliances and ended with his death. His brother Teimuraz later reorganized the eastern power.

Son of Vajtang V, he was installed at different times in Kajetia and Imereti. His repeated losses of the throne led him to Russian exile, where he developed his literary activity. He unites the three territorial branches without turning them into a single permanent crown.

name: Bearne
summary: Béarn was a viscounty with institutions and legal traditions of its own. Margaret of Montcada’s inheritance linked it to the counts of Foix without erasing those differences. Gaston Fébus maintained a particularly strong degree of autonomy. After his death, the inheritance passed to the Castellbò branch and then to the descendants of Isabella of Foix and Archambaud of Grailly. Connections with Navarre brought the viscounty to the Albrets and Bourbons. Sharing a ruler with Navarre did not make Béarn part of the Navarrese kingdom; each title and institutional history must be followed separately.

eventos.descripcion: A few days after the wedding of Margarita de Valois and Enrique de Navarra, Coligny's assassination attempt leads to the killing of Huguenot leaders in Paris and a new wave of violence for the kingdom.
The death of Francis of Anjou makes Enrique de Navarra an alleged heir. Enrique de Guisa reorganizes the Catholic League, backed from Spain, to prevent a Protestant from inheriting the French crown.

Henry III is killed after having allied with Henry of Navarre against the League. With his death the Valois-Angulema line on the throne is extinguished and Henry of Navarre claims the crown as Henry IV.

Henry IV’s conversion removes one of the biggest obstacles to his acceptance as king. The League gradually loses support and war ceases to be a simple alternative between a Catholic king and a Protestant.

Henry IV promulgates the Edict of Nantes and grants Protestants civil rights and a limited framework of worship and security. The Bourbon monarchy closes the great phase of the Wars of Religion without imposing complete confessional uniformity.

name: Trebizond
summary: The court of the Grand Komnenoi retained its own imperial identity on the Black Sea. Its position depended on maritime and land trade, relations with Georgia and negotiation with Anatolian powers. Marriages and internal rivalries should be read together with growing Ottoman pressure.
notes: Empire of the Grand Komnenoi of the Black Sea, different from the Byzantine Empire of Constantinople.

He defended the autonomy of his empire against the tutelage of Andronic II and negotiated commercial access for genoese and Venetians. His marriage to Djiadjak Jakeli reinforced the connection with Samtsje and the Georgian elites.
Daughter of Beka I of Samtsje and wife of Alejo II of Trebizond. Andronico II's opposition to this marriage reveals that the family alliances of the Black Sea could contradict Constantinople's plans.

Son of Alejo II, he took power in 1332. His offspring allow him to continue the imperial genealogy until Alejo III, although this did not happen directly. The court went through several changes of ruler between the two generations.

He came to power in 1349 and was crowned in 1350. His long government reinforced the religious patronage and commercial relations of the empire. Family connections with neighboring powers coexisted with the competition of Italian merchants on the Black Sea.

He ruled between Timur’s pressures and the Ottomans. His marriage to Gulkhan links imperial continuity with Georgia. Trebizond maintained a self-government within a regional scenario of tributes, alliances and trade rivalries.

Georgian princess, took the name Eudoxia and married Manuel III. She was the mother of Alejo IV. Her file connects two Black Sea courts without attributing a territorial government to her for her status as consort.

He succeeded Manuel III and died during the rebellion of his son Juan. Sources disagree about his birth, which is shown as an interval. His marriage to Theodora links the imperial family with the Cantacucenos.

Wife of Alejo IV, she was the mother of John IV and David. Her identity must be distinguished from the same-named empress married to Alejo III. Registering both unions as one would produce an impossible genealogy.

He reached the throne during the rebellion against his father. His government faced increasing Ottoman pressure on the Black Sea routes. Genoese documentation allows him to place his death in 1460, before David's access.

Last emperor of Trebizond, he sought external support before the Ottoman conquest of 1461. He was executed in 1463. The loss of government and his death were different events; the record retains both dates.

name: Saluzzo

persona.resumen: Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire and sovereign of a composite monarchy that reached the Iberian peninsula, Italy, the Netherlands and America. Philip I inherited the Franche-Comté, Artois, Namur and Luxembourg, as well as other Dutch territories. He later incorporated Frisia, Utrecht, Overijssel, Drente, Groningen and Guelders in a staggered form, between 1524 and 1543. He preserved the ducal dignity of Burgundy, but did not rule the Duchy incorporated into France. From 1535 he kept Milan under imperial control; the investiture and subsequent possession of Philip II must be distinguished from that government.

The son of Cathal Crobderg, he defended his position in Connacht by negotiating and fighting both with other Gaelic candidates and with the Anglo-Normans. His government shows the survival of a regional monarchy after the conquest begun in the 12th century.

He succeeded his father Fedlimid and fought the Burgh expansion in Connacht. His victory in Áth an Chip in 1270 temporarily stopped his advance. Disputes between branches of his own family continued after his death.

persona.resumen: Chief of the O’Neill who accepted the title of Earl of Tyrone in 1542. The agreement with Henry VIII did not eliminate Gaelic succession or family disputes: both systems legitimized different candidates.

He defended his election as head of the O’Neill against the successor system of Earldom of Tyrone. He alternated war and negotiation with Elizabeth I, and contested the dominance of Northern Ireland over other Gaelic houses.

He combined the English title of Count with the Gaelic leadership of the O’Neills. He led the coalition of the Nine Years War, sought Spanish support and ended up exiled after the Fugue of the Counts of 1607.

personas.resumen: Chief of the O’Neill who accepted the title of Earl of Tyrone in 1542. The agreement with Henry VIII did not eliminate Gaelic succession or family disputes: both systems legitimized different candidates.

Recognized by Conn Bacach as the county’s son and heir, he was rejected by Shane O’Neill and murdered by his supporters. His fatherhood was discussed: the recognized bond is preserved, pointing to that uncertainty.

Brother of Hugh O’Neill and father of Owen Roe, he links the generation of the Nine Years’ War with that of the Irish Confederation. His family maintained military and marriage connections between Ulster and the continent.

After a long career in the Spanish armies, he returned to Ireland to lead the forces of the Confederate Ulster. His victory in Benburb reinforced his prestige, but political divisions limited cooperation with other Catholic and realistic leaders.

He participated in the rebellion of 1641 and in the initial organization of his forces in Ulster. Owen Roe’s arrival changed the military leadership. After the parliamentary conquest he was tried and executed, in the closing of the Confederate resistance.
